fields.title: Polka: the feed that won't open
fields.summary: The feed opens in 6.1 seconds on p95 with a target of 1.5. Decide what to pay for speed.
fields.decisionPrompt: How do we speed up the feed? Name the cost of your decision.
fields.brief/role: You are the Polka product manager.
fields.brief/company: Polka is a fictional local grocery delivery service: 900 partner stores, buyer app, and partner dashboard.
fields.brief/context: You are the Polka product manager. The main app screen — a feed with recommendations and items from nearby stores — opens in 2.8 seconds on median and 6.1 on p95. The target metric set in quarterly goals is 1.5 seconds on p95. The screen is assembled from six sources: catalog, stock, prices, store ratings, user history, recommendations. This week, an approach must be chosen.
fields.brief/objective: Meet the target 1.5 seconds on p95 without turning speed into incorrect data on the screen.
fields.brief/constraints: A week left in the quarter. Six sources on the screen, cannot rewrite them all at once.
fields.brief/task: Choose an approach to speed up and name what you pay for it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Data is denormalized when its discrepancy goes unnoticed
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Fast reads are bought by data duplication, and the price paid is desync. Therefore, the choice isn't driven by the magnitude of gain, but by the price of discrepancy: a rating outdated by an hour is unnoticeable, but a stock count outdated by minutes is seen by the user at checkout and perceived as deceit. First ask what happens when the copy lags behind, and only then — by how many milliseconds it gets faster.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content: Catalog 180 ms, recommendations 240 ms, history 120 ms, store ratings 890 ms, stock 1,100 ms, prices 260 ms. The rest is network and rendering.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content: "Ratings are calculated on the fly across all store reviews — hence 890 ms. Stock is read from the relational database via one query per store, up to 12 stores in the feed. We can put rating and stock directly into the catalog product card — the feed will become a single query, about 400 ms total."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content: An item runs out on average 2.3 times a day per store. Between deliveries, stock changes every 4–7 minutes during working hours.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content: 11% of requests are "item disappeared at checkout". This is already happening now, with honest stock reads.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Denormalize everything: rating and stock into the catalog card
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Two weeks. Feed is a single query, about 400 ms.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence: target is reached with headroom. Stock in the catalog lags by minutes. The share of "item disappeared" complaints will grow — by how much is unknown, but mechanically, people adding missing items will increase.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Denormalize only rating, keep stock honest
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: One week. Rating is a materialized view recalculated hourly. Feed around 1.9 seconds on p95.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence: target is not met, but substantial improvement — from 6.1 to 1.9. Rating lags by an hour, which no one will notice. Stock is honest, complaint share does not grow. The stock task remains for next quarter.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Denormalize rating, read stock via a single batch query
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Three weeks. Instead of 12 queries, one for all stores at once. Feed around 1.4 seconds on p95.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence: target is met. Stock is honest. More expensive in time, requires rewriting the stock access layer. Risk: batch query is heavier for the database, effect on the evening peak must be checked.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Show feed without stock, load them after rendering
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: A week and a half. Screen appears in 900 ms, availability badges appear a second later.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence: formally the target is met — screen is rendered. Stock is honest. User sees a "jumping" interface, some cards are marked out of stock a second later. Metric improves, feeling — not necessarily.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Does not distinguish safe and dangerous duplication
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Does not see that the number of queries matters more than the speed of each
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Did not connect data lag with user perception
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Does not see that data duplication is a choice, not an optimization
